name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Deliver: Push link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day (the access gate)

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Require every PR to include a link to the ticket it closes.

This forces engineers to connect code changes to business value, making coverage measurable. The trade-off is extra friction—some PRs will feel trivial—but it guarantees we never lose track of why we wrote the code. Without this, link coverage stays a guessing game.

name: Scriv
text: The ticket-link rule trades real friction for a false sense of coverage—broken links still count as "covered" if the PR mentions the ticket number, and engineers will game the system by pasting dead URLs. A better lever is to measure *actual* link health: run a daily crawler that flags 404s and 301s, then auto-block merges until the PR fixes its own broken references. That settles the argument by making the gate real, not performative.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Implement a daily automated link health check to verify the status of all links associated with PRs. This ensures that only functional links contribute to our coverage metrics, improving the accuracy of our measurement. The trade-off is the initial investment in development time and potential daily operational overhead, but this approach guarantees we maintain meaningful and reliable link coverage, directly supporting our goal of pushing toward 100% daily.

name: Sift
text: The real risk here is that the daily automated link health check becomes a bureaucratic hurdle, where engineers spend more time troubleshooting crawler false positives than actually writing code. A better alternative might be to implement a simpler, manual link verification step during the PR review process, which would allow human judgment to filter out genuine issues from minor glitches. What would settle this argument is data on how often broken links actually occur versus the cost of developing and maintaining the automated crawler.
